burnham-plan-whitehall-risk-averse.headline: Labour MPs fear Burnham's 10-year plan is not radical enough; top civil servant calls Whitehall 'tame'
burnham-plan-whitehall-risk-averse.body_md:
Andy Burnham's government has promised a 10-year plan to remake how Britain is run. Two reports now suggest it faces doubt from two directions at once. Labour backbenchers fear it will not be radical enough, and the country's most senior civil servant has reportedly said the machinery meant to deliver it is too timid.

Both accounts come from Guardian Politics headlines. The full texts were not available when this piece was written, so the detail below rests on the headlines and on earlier reporting of the plan. No MP is named here, and nothing is quoted beyond the headline wording.

## The backbench worry

The headline says Labour MPs fear the plan will not go far enough. That fits a pattern that predates this report. The New Statesman has [reported](https://www.newstatesman.com/politics/uk-politics/2026/09/labour-mps-pressure-burnham-over-reindustrialisation) that Burnham faces the same soft-left pressure that dogged his predecessor, from MPs who hoped a new prime minister would be as radical in office as he once promised to be. Separately, about 80 Labour MPs have urged him to "turn rhetoric into reality" and keep the promises he made on the road to No 10, according to [one account](https://www.blackcountryradio.co.uk/news/politics-news/labour-mps-form-new-squad-to-ensure-burnham-keeps-key-pledge/).

The worry has also been fed by what is known of the plan itself. One report said it was expected to be a speech plus a slimmed-down document, after suggestions that it might be less ambitious than first thought. Burnham has acknowledged that publication may slip from December into the new year. The New Statesman reported that some inside government fear the exercise could become another case of "kicking the can".

The headline gives no vote, letter or on-record quote. Unease of this kind is common in any governing party. It matters here because the plan is the prime minister's main statement of what the government is for, and a wide gap between that statement and his own backbenchers' hopes would narrow his room for manoeuvre.

## 'Tame' Whitehall

The second thread is the civil service. The Guardian headline has the cabinet secretary, the head of the civil service, calling Whitehall too "tame, reactive and risk-averse". The wording should be checked against the full article. The speaker's position is the point: this is an insider's verdict, not an opposition attack.

It also echoes the prime minister's own framing. Burnham has cast the state as part of the problem. He has promised the "biggest rebalancing of power our country has seen" and has said Whitehall must accept that growth cannot be ordered from the top down. He has also said, in the [Civil Service World report](https://www.civilserviceworld.com/news/article/burnham-pm-departments-compelled-aid-local-authorities-staff-resources), that departments will be compelled to help local authorities with staff and resources. Departments that are cautious by habit would make that harder to deliver.

## Two doubts, one problem

The two criticisms sound different but point the same way. Backbenchers doubt the ambition of the plan. The head of the civil service doubts the capacity of the institution that must carry it out. Between them they leave the government short of both a bold enough design and a bold enough delivery system.

Outside Labour the attack is simpler. Reform UK has dismissed the plan as "a load of waffle" and argued that [Britain cannot wait 10 years](https://londonlovesbusiness.com/reform-savages-burnhams-dream-warning-britain-cant-wait-10-years/). A long horizon gives a government cover to be patient, but it also invites the charge that nothing will change soon.

## What to watch

The first marker is the publication date, and whether the plan arrives before Christmas or slips into the new year. The second is its content: whether it contains dated, costed commitments that satisfy the 80-odd MPs pressing for action, or a statement of direction that leaves them unconvinced. The third is whether the cabinet secretary's remarks are followed by changes to how departments are run, or stay a candid aside. Until the Guardian text and named sources are confirmed, how far this unease reaches inside the party remains unproven.

school-phone-ban-tightened.headline: Phones to be banned from pupils' bags and pockets in English schools
school-phone-ban-tightened.body_md:
England's schools are being pushed towards a stricter line on mobile phones. Under the plan reported by the BBC, pupils would no longer be allowed to carry phones in their bags or pockets during the school day, a step beyond the guidance that has applied since early 2024. The full wording, start date and enforcement arrangements were not available when this article was written, and the detail below is limited accordingly.

## From guidance to rule

The current position dates from February 2024, when the Department for Education (DfE) issued guidance advising schools in England to prohibit phone use for the whole school day, breaks and lunch included. That guidance was not statutory. It told headteachers what the government expected, but it did not oblige them to do so, and it left the method to each school.

That latitude produced a patchwork. Some schools collect phones at the gate or lock them in pouches. Others ask pupils to keep devices out of sight, which in practice means in a bag or a pocket. The new approach appears aimed at that second category. A phone that is switched off but still on the pupil's person is, on this reading, still a phone in school.

The distinction matters because a rule about use is difficult to police. A teacher must catch the device in the act. A rule about possession is easier to apply: either the phone is in the bag or it is not.

## What is not yet clear

The central question is whether the change will be statutory. If it is written into law or binding regulations, phone-free policy would become something schools must follow rather than something they are advised to follow, and it would be open to inspection and challenge. If it is strengthened guidance, it would be tougher in tone but would leave heads with the same discretion as before.

Several other points remain unconfirmed:

- the date from which schools would be expected to comply;
- how compliance would be checked, including any role for Ofsted, the schools inspectorate;
- how exceptions would work for pupils who need a phone for medical reasons, such as monitoring diabetes, or for those with caring responsibilities;
- what schools should do with phones that are handed in, and who is liable if one is lost or damaged.

The last two have been the practical sticking points wherever strict bans have been tried. Storage lockers and pouches cost money, and parents often object to being unable to reach a child in an emergency.

## Why it matters beyond England

Phone restrictions in schools have spread quickly across countries in recent years, with national and regional governments tending to move from advice to compulsion once voluntary approaches prove uneven. England is following that pattern. A legally enforceable rule covering bags and pockets would be among the more demanding versions, and other education systems weighing their own policies may look to how it works in practice.

The economic stakes are small. This is a domestic education measure with little direct market relevance. The political stakes are larger, since the policy is popular with many parents and teachers but raises questions about enforcement that fall on school leaders.

## What to watch

The test is in the text. The DfE's announcement, and any accompanying consultation or draft legislation, should show whether the rule is statutory, when it starts and who polices it. Reaction from head teachers' unions to the enforcement and cost questions will show how workable the plan is.
school-phone-ban-tightened.in_one_sentence: England is moving from voluntary school phone guidance towards a stricter rule covering pupils' bags and pockets, though whether it will be statutory is not yet confirmed.

us-congress-leadership-hegseth.headline: Thune stays Senate GOP leader, Jordan beats Scalise for House minority leader; Hegseth impeachment bid blocked for now
us-congress-leadership-hegseth.body_md:
House Republicans have chosen Jim Jordan, the Ohio hardliner who chairs the Judiciary Committee, to lead them in opposition. They passed over Steve Scalise, the sitting majority leader. In a closed-door, secret-ballot vote on Tuesday, Jordan won 106 to 73. Senate Republicans, meeting separately, kept John Thune as their leader. The same day the House voted to shelve an attempt to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.

## A conference picks its temperament

The House vote follows a midterm election in which Republicans lost control of the chamber. Reporting on the vote put the party's losses at more than 40 seats. Mike Johnson is stepping aside as the party's leader. That left a contest between two men who have long sat at the centre of the conference, each with a different claim on it. Scalise has been the party's number two for years and runs the floor. Jordan is better known as a confrontational investigator and a favourite of the party's more combative wing.

The margin was wide, though not overwhelming. The 179 votes cast split 106 to 73. A leader who loses the majority generally has less to manage and more to oppose, and the conference appears to have decided that Jordan suits that task. His committee has been the House Republicans' main vehicle for oversight fights. When Democrats take the gavels in January, the minority's tools will be messaging, procedural resistance and whatever pressure can be brought on the new majority's investigations.

This is also a precedent worth noting. In 2018, after the last midterm loss of this kind, Jordan challenged Kevin McCarthy for the same post and lost 159 to 43. Eight years on, he has won the same job against a more senior rival.

## Thune holds the Senate

The Senate result was quieter. Thune was re-elected leader by acclamation, according to his spokesperson. Some senators had asked for the vote to be delayed, but no challenger emerged. That sets his position for the next Congress, although the tallies and circumstances in the Senate conference are less documented than the House count.

The contrast is part of the story. The Senate conference reaffirmed its leader without a contest, while the House conference replaced its own number two for the top job after a rout.

## Hegseth impeachment put off

The House also dealt with Republican Thomas Massie's resolution to impeach Hegseth. Massie, a Kentucky Republican, had filed eight articles, centred on the Iran war and alleged violations of war powers law. The House voted 211 to 204 to refer the resolution to committee, which in practice shelves it. Massie was the only Republican to vote with all the Democrats against the motion.

That ends the effort for now, not for good. The measure was never likely to succeed in a Republican-controlled House. Reports note that the delay may only postpone the matter. Democrats take control of the House in January, and they will decide whether to revive the accusations. They will do so facing a Republican minority led by Jordan.

## What comes next

The immediate test is January, when the new Congress is sworn in and the leadership change takes effect. Whether Democrats revisit Hegseth's conduct, and how Jordan's conference responds, will show more clearly what the 106 to 73 vote bought. Details of the tallies come from reporting by PBS NewsHour, ABC News, NBC News and The Hill, rather than from conference records.

sas-inquiry-new-photos.headline: New photographs are 'essential evidence' of possible SAS war crimes, inquiry told
sas-inquiry-new-photos.body_md:
The statutory inquiry into alleged unlawful killings by British special forces in Afghanistan has published, for the first time, photographs taken after two SAS night raids in Helmand province in 2011. Its lead barrister told the hearing they may be evidence of possible war crimes. The photographs move the inquiry from competing accounts of what happened inside Afghan homes towards physical evidence that can be tested.

## What the photographs show

The images were released on Tuesday. According to the BBC's report, they show multiple people lying in beds with head wounds across the two operations. One person lies under a floral blanket. Others have their heads on pillows, with blood pooling around them. Blood spatter low on one wall is described as consistent with someone being shot while lying down.

Oliver Glasgow KC, counsel to the inquiry, said many of the dead "look like they sustained head shots" and that one body appears to have its head on a pillow. Further analysis, he said, might confirm whether people were "shot when asleep." The inquiry is putting the photographs through expert forensic analysis. The BBC report does not name the experts.

Seventeen people were killed across the two operations. The youngest victims were 15 and 14 years old, one in each raid. The SAS was working alongside Afghan special forces on night raids against the Taliban.

## Two accounts of the same raids

The official special forces account is that insurgents fired on troops as they entered the compounds, and that the SAS returned fire. The photographs sit uneasily with that.

The BBC's Panorama programme examined four raids on homes that killed 26 people. Weapons experts consulted for that investigation said the evidence suggested multiple rounds were fired from above, which would indicate the victims were lying down or sitting against a wall rather than caught in a firefight. Relatives told the programme their family members had been shot cleanly in the head or chest. Panorama's 2022 investigation led to the inquiry being set up that year. It examines allegations that the SAS murdered unarmed civilians and detainees on night raids between 2010 and 2013, and planted weapons to cover the killings up. Counsel's remarks are allegations and questions for expert analysis. They are not findings.

## The question of why they were not tested

The inquiry also heard that these images are not entirely new to the state. Lt Col John Harvey, who led the military police murder investigation, agreed the photographs "didn't look right" and said his team regarded them as potentially vital evidence. Investigators repeatedly asked for them to be submitted for further testing. That never happened.

An anonymous investigator told the BBC that low bullet marks on the walls seemed to contradict the special forces' version of events. The inquiry also heard that investigators were still in Afghanistan in July 2019, looking for eyewitnesses, when senior officers were preparing to close the murder investigation and inform ministers. A member of the Afghan partner unit told military police he had personally seen a British soldier plant a rifle on an unarmed person after they had been killed.

The Ministry of Defence has said two independent investigations have examined the conduct of British forces in Afghanistan and that neither found sufficient evidence to prosecute. The inquiry's task is partly to test that conclusion, and the untested photographs bear directly on it. The sequence the hearing described is that investigators saw the images as important, asked for expert work, and did not get it.

## What comes next

The inquiry is already under strain from its volume of material. In September the Ministry of Defence disclosed about 97 million further documents, which the chair, Lord Justice Haddon-Cave, has treated as a cause of further delay and cost. He has also said the inquiry holds some 10,000 photographs from the raids that appear not to have formed part of the military police investigation. The forensic results on the 2011 images will show whether the sleeping-victim hypothesis survives expert scrutiny. If it does, the question of why the evidence went untested will move to the centre of the inquiry's examination of the investigation itself.

us-soldier-russia-spy-arrest-uk.headline: US soldier arrested in UK on suspicion of spying for Russia; three Iran-backed suspects accused of plots
us-soldier-russia-spy-arrest-uk.body_md:
Two counter-intelligence cases, one Russian and one Iranian, have put American personnel and British military sites on the same page this autumn. On Tuesday, counter-terrorism police arrested a 41-year-old US Army soldier near Gloucester on suspicion of offences related to Russia. Two weeks earlier, two men were charged over an alleged Iran-directed plot at RAF Fairford, the Gloucestershire base US bombers had been using. Neither case has come to trial, and nobody has been convicted of anything.

The headline's reference to "three suspects" in Iran-linked plots needs qualifying. The reporting reviewed for this article shows two men charged over Fairford. A third man, a 25-year-old dual British-Iranian national, was re-arrested on 20 October on suspicion of assisting Iran's intelligence service and released without charge. He remains on police bail. The charges against him are not established.

## The soldier at Imjin Barracks

The Metropolitan Police said the man was arrested on Tuesday near Gloucester as part of a Counter Terrorism Policing investigation. He is held at a London police station. He has not been named, and his name is expected to emerge only if he is formally charged. Police searched two addresses in Gloucestershire. A source told ABC News he was stationed at Imjin Barracks, home of NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps headquarters, where a small US intelligence contingent helps process some of the alliance's intelligence.

He was arrested on suspicion of offences under Sections 1 and 3 of the National Security Act 2023, the law that covers espionage and foreign interference. British authorities said: "The country to which the allegations relate is Russia." Police said the case is not linked to other Counter Terrorism Policing investigations.

The US side has been unusually open about its involvement. Brig. Gen. Sean Stinchon, who leads US Army Counterintelligence Command, called him a "senior soldier" and described the arrest as "a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent." He thanked UK and FBI colleagues for their teamwork. FBI Director Kash Patel said the case "involves allegations of espionage, which is of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies." A source told ABC that he may also face action from the US Army. The specific charges remain unclear.

## Fairford: from vans to charges

The Iranian case has a longer paper trail. In the early hours of 27 September, armed police and army bomb-disposal teams converged on a rural area near RAF Fairford after reports of suspicious vans heading towards the base. Five British men were arrested outside it. US bombers, which had used Fairford for strikes on Iran, were withdrawn on security grounds shortly afterwards.

On 27 October, prosecutors charged two of those held, both 24, under the National Security Act:

- **Mohmed Abdulkarim**, a British national, is charged with conduct likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence service between 31 August and 28 September. Police say the country is believed to be Iran.
- **Nouman Essghir**, a dual British-Iranian national, is charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK on 22 August.

Six other people remain on police bail. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the activity was likely coordinated in Iran, and the government's position has been that the Revolutionary Guard was almost certainly behind it. Iran's ambassador has denied involvement. Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of National Counter Terrorism Policing, said: "We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state."

## A pattern, or two files on one desk?

The two cases differ in almost every operational respect. One involves an alleged insider with access to alliance intelligence, apparently working for Moscow. The other involves outsiders, mostly young British men, accused of reconnaissance and possible hostile action against a base for Tehran. The Met has said the soldier's case is unconnected to its other investigations, and nothing published ties the two together.

What they share is a target set. Both involve American military activity on British soil, one at a NATO headquarters and one at an airfield used in an active conflict. Both are being handled under the National Security Act 2023, which gives police and prosecutors broader tools than the old Official Secrets regime. The US Army's public thanks to MI5, Defence Counter Intelligence and the FBI suggest that allied cooperation, rather than a single agency, produced the arrest.

That is an inference from the pattern of official statements, not a finding. Hostile services have long taken an interest in US bases in Britain. What is new is how many such cases are reaching the public in a short space of time, and that charges rather than leaks now define them.

## What to watch

The first marker is whether the soldier is charged and named, which should show which sections of the Act are in play and whether the US pursues its own case. For Fairford, the next steps are the committal of Abdulkarim and Essghir and a decision on whether the third man and the six on bail are charged. A charging decision in either case will test whether the Russian and Iranian threads stay separate or start to overlap.

casey-social-care-no-one-in-charge.headline: 'No one is in charge': Louise Casey to say social care in England is in chaos
casey-social-care-no-one-in-charge.body_md:
Social care in England has no clear owner, and that is the central charge Baroness Louise Casey is set to level at the system, according to the Guardian's account of her forthcoming remarks. Her reported words are blunt: "no one is in charge." The finding is a political problem as much as an administrative one, because any fix would fall on a Treasury and an NHS that are both under budget pressure.

A note on sourcing belongs at the outset. This article rests on a single outlet's headline and summary. The full text of Casey's remarks and the commission's published findings could not be checked, and no figures, dates or report title were available. Everything below that goes beyond the reported quotation is context, not confirmed detail of the new findings.

## What is being claimed

The reported claim is structural. Social care covers help with washing, dressing, eating and living independently for older and disabled adults, delivered mostly by private providers and commissioned by local councils. It is not part of the NHS, and responsibility is split among central government departments, councils, the NHS and providers. "No one is in charge" is a statement about that division of responsibility, not about any single failing.

Casey, a crossbench peer and former government adviser, is understood to lead the Independent Commission on adult social care that the government set up in 2025. As far as can be established from earlier announcements, it was designed to report in stages, with a first phase ahead of a fuller set of recommendations later. Readers should check the commission's own publications for the exact remit and timetable, as these could not be verified here.

## Why the Treasury and the NHS are implicated

The Guardian's framing is that the findings add pressure on both. The link is plausible, though the evidence for it in this case is not yet in hand. Hospitals have long reported patients who are medically fit to leave but cannot, because a care package or a care-home place is not available. That ties a stalled care system to hospital capacity, a point commonly made by NHS leaders. Whether Casey's findings quantify it is unknown.

The Treasury's exposure is simpler. Any reform that gives one body clear ownership of social care, or raises pay, standards or eligibility, costs money, and the public finances are already tight. The cross-links elsewhere in this edition show the wider backdrop: higher government borrowing costs and a Bank of England signalling that rates may stay elevated.

## What to watch

Three things will settle how far the story travels. First, whether the commission names a single accountable body, and which department or authority it proposes. Second, whether it attaches costings, since a diagnosis without a price tag lets ministers defer. Third, how the government responds, and whether any of it surfaces in fiscal statements rather than only in a consultation.

Until the report's text is available, the reported finding is best read as a pointed assertion from a credible figure, not a documented conclusion. The substance of the argument depends on evidence that has yet to be checked.
casey-social-care-no-one-in-charge.in_one_sentence: Louise Casey is reported to say no one is in charge of social care in England, a finding that would add pressure on the Treasury and NHS, though the report itself is unchecked.

world-in-brief-spy-haiti.headline: Acquitted 'China spy' says he was a fall guy; El Salvador claims Haitian gang HQ destroyed
world-in-brief-spy-haiti.body_md:
Two unrelated claims, both made by interested parties and neither independently confirmed, led the BBC's world and politics feeds on Wednesday. In Britain, a man acquitted in a case billed as a "China spy" prosecution says he was a fall guy for the security services. In the Caribbean, El Salvador's president says his forces have destroyed a Haitian gang's headquarters.

In both cases the public record is thinner than the headlines suggest. The Tribune has been unable to retrieve the court, charges, dates or the defendant's name for the UK case, and has found no independent account of the Haiti strike.

## An acquittal and an accusation

The defendant was acquitted in a UK prosecution described as a China-spying case. He now alleges he was made a "fall guy" for the security services. That is his account, not a finding by any court or inquiry. Nothing seen so far shows what the security services say in reply, and the claim cannot be tested without the trial record.

It lands in territory that is already sensitive. In September 2025 the Crown Prosecution Service dropped Official Secrets Act charges against Christopher Cash and Christopher Berry weeks before their trial. The Director of Public Prosecutions said prosecutors could not obtain government evidence describing China as a national security threat. The Home Secretary denied any ministerial interference, and MI5's director general, Ken McCallum, voiced frustration at the outcome. Separately, a jury at the Old Bailey has convicted two men, a former police superintendent and an immigration officer, of assisting Chinese intelligence by spying on Hong Kong dissidents.

Those cases are not this one, and nothing retrieved links them to the acquitted man's claim. They show why such allegations draw attention. China-related prosecutions in Britain are rare, politically charged and dependent on evidence that agencies and ministers control. If the man's claim were substantiated, it would suggest the security services shaped a prosecution, and that would affect trust in such cases. Until the verdict, the court record and any official response are checked, it remains an assertion by a defendant who has reason to make it.

## El Salvador's claim in Haiti

President Nayib Bukele says Salvadoran forces destroyed a Haitian gang headquarters. The BBC is the only listed source, and the claim comes from Bukele himself, not from independent or on-the-ground reporting.

The context is a deployment of more than 2,000 Salvadoran troops and military hardware, ordered after four Salvadoran aviation technicians disappeared following a gang attack on 18 October. They have not been found. Bukele has said the aim is to recover them, not to occupy Haiti. The UN says only about 200 of the Salvadoran soldiers fall under the jurisdiction of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force. Haiti's prime minister, Alix Didier Fils-Aimé, says foreign forces operate under Haitian authority.

Earlier this month Bukele said Salvadoran helicopters had fired on gangs attacking Chadian soldiers of the force, and posted: "The gangs no longer have the upper hand." Haitian police, working with the force and Salvadoran troops, found the burned remains of a truck they said the missing men's group had used, in Croix-des-Bouquets.

Bukele has a record of publicising operations on social media, and his state of emergency at home has drawn criticism from rights groups. The UN has urged that all operations respect human rights law. Médecins Sans Frontières reported 30 people injured, including women and children, in the eight days after 18 October, and warned that more international forces could worsen the situation. Haiti has had no elected government since 2021, and elections have been pushed back to July 2027.

## What to watch

For the UK case, the questions are the court record, the charges, and whether the security services or the Crown Prosecution Service respond to the allegation. For Haiti, they are Haitian police or UN confirmation of what was struck and who was inside, and whether the four missing technicians are found.
world-in-brief-spy-haiti.in_one_sentence: An acquitted UK defendant calls himself a security-services fall guy and Bukele says Haiti's gang HQ is destroyed, but both claims are unverified.

robot-minehunters.headline: Robot vessels take on dangerous mine-hunting work
robot-minehunters.body_md:
The most dangerous job in naval warfare may be one of the least visible. Clearing sea mines means finding explosive devices that are often built to be hard to find, then disabling or destroying them without setting them off. For decades that has meant crewed minehunters, small ships with specialised hulls, and clearance divers working close to live charges. Navies are now handing more of that work to vessels with nobody on board.

The idea is simple. A small uncrewed boat, controlled from a ship or from shore, tows a sonar or launches an underwater drone to search for mines. If it finds one, it can mark the position or deploy a device to destroy it. The crew stays well outside the area where a mine could go off.

This piece draws on a BBC Business report. The article's specific figures, names and dates could not be independently confirmed at the time of writing, so what follows is the general picture rather than a report of that article's detail.

## Why the work is being moved

Mines are cheap compared with the ships they threaten, and they can close a shipping lane or a port long before a shot is fired. A single suspected mine can stop traffic until someone proves the water is safe. Crewed minehunters are built to survive nearby blasts, with non-magnetic hulls and quiet engines, but they are still ships with sailors aboard, and they are slow, expensive and ageing in several fleets.

Several navies, including those of the UK and the US, have spent recent years developing or fielding uncrewed mine-countermeasure systems. The UK has worked with France on a joint programme in this area, and the US Navy has invested in uncrewed systems for its own mine-countermeasure needs. Current programme status should be checked against official sources, as schedules in this field have a history of slipping.

## The reliability question

Taking sailors out of the minefield only helps if the robots do the job. A crewed minehunter can be trusted, in part, because its crew can see something odd and change course. A mine-hunting drone has to do the same with a sonar image and a software model of what a mine looks like.

There are two ways it can go wrong. If a system misses a mine, a ship may be sent through water that is not safe. If it flags too many harmless objects as threats, clearing a lane takes so long that the speed advantage disappears. Seabeds are cluttered with rocks, wrecks and debris, so false alarms are a real cost.

Communications are another weak point. A vessel that depends on a radio link to a controller can be jammed, and a long mission needs reliable power and enough autonomy to keep working if the link drops.

## What is at stake

If the technology works at scale, navies could cut the risk to crews and might spend less on maintaining fleets of ageing minehunters. That would shift money towards the defence contractors that build the boats, sonars and software, which is why the story sits in a business section. It would also mean a navy could replace crewed ships before the uncrewed alternative has proved itself, a gap that leaves it exposed if a mine threat arrives early.

The next real signals are the trials and acceptance tests in the programmes that already exist, and in particular whether the uncrewed systems can clear a lane to the standard that commanders require before they will send in a merchant or warship. Until that is shown, the crewed minehunters are likely to stay in service alongside the robots rather than disappear.
robot-minehunters.in_one_sentence: Navies are shifting mine clearance to uncrewed vessels to keep sailors out of minefields, but the shift only pays off if the robots prove as reliable as crewed minehunters.

kenya-el-nino-floods.headline: Kenya braces for El Niño floods
kenya-el-nino-floods.body_md:
Kenya's weather service says the coming short rains are likely to be wetter than normal across the whole country, and the El Niño behind that outlook is forecast to be very strong. Flood warnings are now out for East Africa. The harder question is whether anyone acts on them early enough to matter.

The forecasts are firm, but the most recent material found for this article dates from early September, so what follows does not capture the latest official position.

## What the forecasts say

The Kenya Meteorological Department (KMD) has put the probability that the 2026 El Niño turns out very strong at 81%. It puts the chance that the event lasts into the first months of 2027 at 97%. Its national outlook for the October–December short rains, issued on 26 August, gives some areas an 85–90% likelihood of above-normal rainfall. Its 10 September update warned of floods, flash floods and landslides. Some counties were expected to see enhanced rain as early as September, with wet conditions possibly running into early 2027.

The Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) took a more mixed view in July. It said strong short rains should improve pasture in pastoral areas, but it also flagged flood risk. The World Food Programme has made the same point about timing: millions of Kenyans are still recovering from a severe drought, and floods would hit communities that have little left to absorb them.

## Not a repeat of 1997–98, necessarily

The 1997–98 El Niño is the benchmark for flood damage in Kenya, and comparisons to it were always going to be made. KMD has cautioned against drawing them automatically. El Niño does not guarantee heavy rain everywhere. The Indian Ocean Dipole, the temperature gradient across that ocean, can strengthen or dampen its effects in East Africa. This year a positive dipole is reported to be adding to the El Niño signal, which is why the seasonal outlook leans so wet.

A seasonal forecast gives odds for a three-month period. It does not say which river will burst, or when. That gap is where preparedness is tested.

## From forecast to action

The government has activated a national framework. It is coordinated by the National Disaster Risk Management Authority and overseen by an Ad Hoc Cabinet Committee on El Niño Preparedness and Response, and the deputy president has publicly said the country is ready.

The things that decide outcomes are mostly local and unglamorous: whether drains and culverts are cleared before the rains, whether families on floodplains and steep slopes are moved in time, whether stocks of food and medicines are in place before roads are cut, and whether funding is released on a forecast rather than after the damage. Aid agencies and insurers are watching the last point most closely. Money that arrives after the floods pays for relief. Money that arrives before them can reduce the losses.

No death toll, damage estimate or confirmed rainfall totals for this season were found, and none are reported here.

## What to watch

The next markers are KMD's monthly and weekly updates as the short rains build, and the speed of any evacuation orders and emergency releases in flood-prone counties. If the wet season runs into early 2027 as forecast, the same systems will be tested again.

nvidia-huang-probe-h200-pla.headline: Nvidia hires a major US law firm as the FBI probes Huang's alleged link to a suspected Chinese spy, and Reuters reports H200s reached a PLA-linked university
nvidia-huang-probe-h200-pla.body_md:
Nvidia's board has opened an inquiry into its own chief executive. The cause is reporting that Jensen Huang had an intimate relationship with a business executive whom US intelligence is said to have judged to be gathering information for Beijing. Nvidia makes the AI chips that Washington most wants to keep out of Chinese military hands. That makes a personal allegation a national-security question for the company.

The brief behind this piece adds two further claims: that President Trump has said the FBI is investigating, and that Nvidia has retained a major US law firm. **Neither could be confirmed in the sources checked for this article.** Nor could the Reuters report that Nvidia H200 chips reached a university linked to the People's Liberation Army. The claims come from BBC and Reuters reporting relayed through summaries. They are set out below as reported, not as established.

## What is on the record

Nvidia's board announced the inquiry on Sunday, 8 November. Huang supports it and is cooperating, and he remains CEO while it runs. According to the New York Times, as relayed by Fox, Huang told the board he had been intimate with a business executive. The paper reported that US intelligence concluded she was passing information directly to Beijing.

The executive is Alice Huang, a top figure at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data-centre company. Reporting identifies her as a Chinese citizen. The coverage reviewed does not say whether she is related to Jensen Huang. Megaspeed has bought about $4.8bn of Nvidia chips over two years, which makes it one of Nvidia's largest customers. The New York Times has also reported that US officials are examining Megaspeed's China ties.

The board said it has "no reason to believe" that national security or Nvidia's secrets were compromised. It said the inquiry "will examine all available information" and that US national and economic security are its top priorities. In a message to staff, reported by the Times, Huang said he had been unfaithful to his wife and was "deeply sorry". China's foreign ministry called the allegations unsubstantiated and described them as smears.

## The FBI and the law firm

The triage brief says Trump has publicly said the FBI is investigating, and that Nvidia has hired an outside US law firm. The BBC is cited as the source. Searches of the available coverage found no FBI statement, no White House transcript and no Nvidia statement naming either. The firm's name is not known. If Trump did say it, that is the step that matters. An FBI inquiry would sit alongside, and could override, the board's own review, and it would bring Nvidia's leadership into the export-control debate.

It also bears on how much weight a board review can carry. A company investigating its own chief executive is not independent. Outside counsel is the usual way boards try to supply independence, but that only works if the firm reports to directors and not to management.

## Congress and the chips

The parallel pressure is already documented. Representatives Brian Mast, John Moolenaar and Rick Crawford have invited Huang to a joint briefing on 18 November, the day after Nvidia's quarterly results. They want answers on his contacts with Alice Huang and on how Nvidia stops foreign espionage. It is not known whether he will attend. Separately, in March, US lawmakers asked whether his remarks on chip smuggling had misled regulators.

The Reuters report belongs here. As relayed in the brief, it says a PLA-linked university bought H200 chips despite being on a US blacklist. The H200 is a restricted chip. I could not locate that specific story. Reuters did report in March that PLA-linked universities, including Beihang and Harbin Institute of Technology, bought Super Micro servers containing restricted Nvidia A100 chips. Those buyers are on the export blacklist. A purchase of H200s by such a buyer would be a more serious case, because it would involve a newer chip that Washington has handled more cautiously. Until the report is checked, it should be treated as unverified.

If it holds, the two stories connect. The first is about who has Huang's ear. The second is about where the chips end up. Together they pose one question: can the company that sells the world's most sought-after AI hardware show that it knows where it goes?

## What to watch

Three dates and documents will settle most of this. Nvidia's results on 17 November may bring management comment on the inquiry. The congressional briefing on 18 November will show whether Huang appears. The third is an on-record statement from the FBI, the White House or Nvidia on the Trump claim and the law firm. Until one arrives, the confirmed position is an internal board inquiry, a congressional request and a company that says nothing was compromised.

duchy-cornwall-tenants-sell-off.headline: Duchy of Cornwall tenants may have to buy farms or leave as Prince William plans sell-off
duchy-cornwall-tenants-sell-off.body_md:
A private estate that has held land across southern and western England since the fourteenth century is preparing to sell some of it. According to a BBC report, the Duchy of Cornwall, which funds Prince William as Duke of Cornwall, plans to sell parts of its holdings. Some tenant farmers could then be left with a choice: buy the farm they rent, or leave. The detail of that choice is what turns a portfolio decision into a rural-policy question. This article relies on the BBC's account. The scale of the sale, the number of tenancies affected and the Duchy's stated reasons have not been independently confirmed.

## An estate, not a public body

The Duchy was created in 1337 by Edward III to provide an income for the monarch's eldest son. It is often confused with the Crown Estate, but the two differ. The Crown Estate's surplus goes to the Treasury and it publishes accounts under a statutory framework. The Duchy is a private estate whose surplus goes to the Prince of Wales to fund his public duties and private life. It is generally described as covering roughly 130,000 acres, much of it farmland, with a large share of its tenants in the South West.

That status shapes how a sale is judged. A Whitehall department disposing of farmland would face parliamentary questions and published rationale. The Duchy answers mainly to its own governance and to the heir it serves, though it does publish an annual report and takes part in the usual conventions of the tenanted-farm sector.

## What 'buy or leave' means on the ground

Tenant farming is a long-running arrangement in English agriculture. A tenant pays rent for land, buildings and the right to work them, often across generations, without the capital tied up in owning the freehold. A landlord that decides to sell can offer the holding to the sitting tenant, sell it on the open market, or sell it with the tenant in place.

The pressure points are plain enough:

- **Price.** A farm's market value is typically far above what a tenant can raise from farm income. Borrowing against land and buildings needs lender confidence at a time of high interest rates.
- **Timing.** A tenant offered first refusal has limited time to arrange finance, valuations and legal work.
- **Security.** The terms of any tenancy, including its length and succession rights, determine whether a tenant who cannot buy can stay under a new owner.

The BBC's framing, as summarised in the headline, is that some tenants may not manage the first option and so face the second. How many are in that position is the figure to establish.

## Why it reaches beyond one estate

The wider interest is in what this does to farm tenure in the South West. Tenanted land is how many people without family land enter farming. If a large landlord moves from letting to selling, that entry route narrows. Land sold to sitting tenants stays in farming under new owners. Land sold on the open market can go to larger neighbours, investors or buyers with no farming plans.

The Duchy has long presented itself as a steward of its tenants and land, with a stated commitment to sustainability. How it squares that stance with a sale that pushes tenants to buy or go will be central to its defence, and its rationale has yet to be tested against the BBC's reporting.

## What to watch

Three things will settle how large this story becomes: the Duchy's own statement on the scope and timetable of the sale, the number of holdings and tenants affected, and the terms offered to those who cannot buy, including any extended tenancies or discounted purchase. Tenant-farming representatives and rural-affairs politicians are likely to press for those details first.
duchy-cornwall-tenants-sell-off.in_one_sentence: The Duchy of Cornwall's reported plan to sell parts of its estate could force some tenant farmers to buy the land they work or leave it.

sport-in-brief-noskova-england.headline: Noskova beats Gauff to reach WTA Finals semi-finals; England squad news on McTominay and Pickford
sport-in-brief-noskova-england.body_md:
Linda Noskova has made the last four of the WTA Finals at her first attempt, and she did it by taking Coco Gauff apart. The Czech won 6-3, 6-3 on Tuesday in their Group 1 match, according to Reuters, and with it she is through to the semi-finals.

## A serve that went missing

Gauff's serve decided it. She won only 43% of points behind her first serve in the opening set, and Noskova broke her five times over the match, four of them in that first set. Both players served nine-ish aces' worth of power — Noskova hit nine, Gauff eight — but Gauff also double-faulted eight times to Noskova's five. Against a hard-hitting opponent in a sprint of a round-robin, that is a costly ledger.

The result was Noskova's second in two group matches. She had already beaten Kostyuk in her opening match, and she has yet to drop a set. Two wins from two guarantees her a place in the knockout stage.

## What is still open

Gauff, on one win and one defeat, is not out. The final round-robin matches on Thursday will settle who joins Noskova from the group, and the standings elsewhere in the draw, including Pegula's chances, are still moving. For Noskova, the remaining group match matters mainly for seeding into the semi-finals, since she cannot be caught for qualification.

It is a notable result for two players in the top tier of the women's game, and a first semi-final at this event for Noskova. It does not change rankings or the structure of the tour, which is why it sits here as a brief.

## A note on the England items

The other half of this cluster does not stand up. Scott McTominay's heart treatment was a pulsed field ablation for a mild arrhythmia, carried out in September while he was at Napoli, and it was widely reported at the time. He plays for Scotland, not England. A report linking his treatment to an England camp, or to Jordan Pickford's goalkeeping competition, could not be confirmed against any source, so neither is reported here as fact.

What to watch: Thursday's final group matches, which determine Gauff's fate and the semi-final pairings.

tories-adhd-benefits-pledge.headline: Tories pledge to cut benefits for children with 'milder' ADHD
tories-adhd-benefits-pledge.body_md:
The Conservatives have said they would stop paying cash disability support to children with what they call milder ADHD, replacing it with other forms of help. Labour has called the plan a "charter for homelessness and human misery". The proposal was announced on 10 November 2026 as part of a wider welfare package. It would link a child's access to cash support to how severe their condition is judged to be, not to the diagnosis alone.

## What is proposed

The benefit at issue is Disability Living Allowance (DLA) for children. According to Big Issue's account of the announcement, the party would replace DLA cash payments for children with milder ADHD, behavioural disorders and learning difficulties with non-cash support. Only the 30% of children with the highest needs would keep the cash. Children with physical disabilities would be protected. Press reports of the announcement say the change would apply to new claims and reassessments.

The Conservatives put the saving at £2.8bn a year, with £1bn of that reinvested in mental health services and family hubs. The measure sits inside a larger plan. Overall, Kemi Badenoch has pledged to cut annual welfare spending by £36.1bn if she becomes prime minister. The figures below come from the party's own announcement as reported, and none has been independently costed.

| Measure | Claimed saving |
|---|---|
| Children's DLA changes | £2.8bn a year |
| All disability-benefit changes (including DLA) | £13.7bn |
| Reinstating the two-child limit | £3.1bn a year |

## The numbers behind it

The policy responds to a steep rise in claims. Big Issue reports that the number of children on DLA rose from 521,476 in 2020 to around 914,000 in 2026. Rising claims do not by themselves show over-diagnosis, and the reports reviewed here do not say how "milder" would be defined or by whom. Part of the increase may reflect better recognition of conditions in children. That is a clinical judgement, and the coverage does not settle it.

Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, defended the approach. As reported, she argued that the current system risks putting children on a "conveyor belt" towards a "lifetime on benefits". Badenoch argued that telling a young person their ADHD means they are defective could be more harmful than the condition itself.

## Reaction

An unnamed Labour spokesperson described the plans as a "charter for homelessness and human misery". The spokesperson warned that they would push families into hardship and cost the state more in emergency support. The spokesperson also said further reforms would follow the Milburn and Timms review. The government has itself launched a review into whether some mental health and neurodivergent conditions are being over-diagnosed, so Labour's objection is to this proposal's scope and not to scrutiny of the system.

Sara Ogilvie, policy director at the Child Poverty Action Group, said the proposals would "take the UK back to the dark ages, causing the biggest overnight increase in child poverty since records began". That is an advocacy group's projection, and the reports do not set out the modelling behind it.

## What to watch

The plan is an opposition pledge, not law, so nothing changes for families now. The questions that would decide its effect are practical ones. These are the clinical or administrative test for "milder", what the non-cash support would consist of, and whether schools and NHS services could deliver it. The Conservatives have not yet said, in the coverage reviewed, who would apply that test. The Milburn and Timms review is the next point at which Labour's own position on children's and mental-health-related benefits may become clearer.

be-ready-stockpiling-toy-sales.headline: Tinned food and bottled water sales jump after 'Be Ready' campaign; toy sales led by stickers and building sets
be-ready-stockpiling-toy-sales.body_md:
A government campaign telling households to be ready for emergencies appears to have done what its designers hoped: people have gone out and bought tins and bottled water. The BBC reports that sales of tinned food and bottled water jumped after the launch of the 'Be Ready' campaign. What it does not yet supply is the size of the jump.

That gap matters. The reported claim is a direction, not a measurement. No retailer data, percentage increase or comparison period has been published in the material seen for this article. Nor is there evidence that the campaign caused the rise rather than coinciding with it. Autumn is a season of its own for stocking the cupboard, and a few weeks of strong sales in a single category can have several explanations.

## What the campaign is, and isn't

'Be Ready' is described as a government preparedness campaign. Its launch date, cost and exact messaging were not stated in the reporting available, so this piece does not characterise them. The sensible reading is the familiar one: official guidance to keep a few days of food, water and basic supplies at home, and shelves that respond to it.

If the shift is real and sustained, it is a small but useful piece of evidence for civil-contingency planners. It would suggest that public messaging can move household behaviour within weeks, and without a crisis to prompt it. For grocers, it would mean a modest, durable lift in some of the dullest and most storable lines in the shop. Both conclusions depend on figures that have yet to appear.

## Meanwhile, in the toy aisle

A second early read on festive spending points the other way, towards the small and cheerful. The BBC's business coverage suggests Christmas toy demand is being carried by stickers and building sets rather than big-ticket presents. The underlying sales data, its provider and any year-on-year comparison were not available to check, so the claim is best taken as a pre-peak impression, not a verdict on the season.

It would, though, fit a familiar pattern. Stickers and brick sets are cheap, easy to wrap and easy to add to a basket, the kind of purchase a household makes while watching its budget. A shopper who is tight on money can still buy a stocking-filler or two.

## One basket, two moods

Put side by side, the two stories make an odd but coherent picture of the household basket in late 2026: a few tins in the cupboard against the day it might be needed, and a pack of stickers for the child who will not be thinking about that. Neither is yet a market story. Both are early, and both lack numbers.

What would change that is data. Retailers' trading updates and the next monthly retail sales figures from the Office for National Statistics are the natural places to see whether tinned food and bottled water stay elevated after the campaign's first burst, and whether the toy aisle's small-ticket strength survives the peak weeks of December.
be-ready-stockpiling-toy-sales.in_one_sentence: Tinned food and bottled water sales reportedly rose after the government's 'Be Ready' campaign, and toys are said to be led by stickers and building sets, but neither claim comes with figures.

ross-walliams-brand-fallout.headline: Jonathan Ross 'horrified' by Walliams allegations and Brand conviction as more allegations reach police
ross-walliams-brand-fallout.body_md:
Jonathan Ross has said he is "horrified" by the allegations against David Walliams and by Russell Brand's conviction. In a statement issued on Tuesday, he said he was once on friendly terms with both men and was "genuinely unaware of their conduct" at the time. The statement lands in an industry still asking who knew what, and when.

## What Ross said

Ross, 65, said he was as horrified as everyone else by the revelations about both men. He also addressed an awkward piece of his own history: a joke at the 2004 Comedy Awards that referred to Walliams and a 15-year-old. Ross said the awards' scriptwriting team wrote the line. He understood it to be a gag about Walliams dating younger women. He called it "tasteless" and said he would not make it today.

The statement followed an ITV News and Guardian investigation, reportedly three years in the making. It sets out multiple allegations of sexual misconduct against Walliams spanning more than two decades. The ITV documentary *David Walliams: Power & Silence* aired on Tuesday night and is available on ITVX and YouTube. One woman describes an encounter at 15 as sexual assault. Several say he groomed them as teenagers. One says he contacted her at 15 after a *Little Britain* fan event, with a sexual relationship starting when she was 17. Other allegations concern conduct linked to *Britain's Got Talent* and his dealings with the publisher HarperCollins.

Walliams denies wrongdoing. In a letter to the journalists, he admitted he "behaved thoughtlessly" towards some casual partners but wrote: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law."

The Metropolitan Police said it was aware of the media reports. It said it had received no related reports of sexual assault or other offences and would assess any that arrived. It has also contacted the media organisations involved in civil proceedings, so that potential victims know how to report to police.

## Brand: conviction and the police

Brand, 51, was convicted on 5 November of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others, in offences between 1999 and 2009. He had denied the charges. The trial involved allegations from six women.

Police are also investigating two further alleged rapes, one involving a girl who was 16 at the time. Met Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley told the BBC that new victims commonly come forward after convictions of well-known figures. "I clearly wouldn't be surprised if many more came forward," he said, adding that a conviction makes people feel that coming forward is possible and that they will be believed. The Reuters report cited here did not give the number of complaints received since the verdict. Reports of the sentence were inconsistent across the sources checked, so none is stated here.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham praised the victims' courage. Asked about a 2014 post of support for Brand, he said he had not known the "full extent" of the behaviour and called the crimes "horrific".

## The industry question

Ross's choice of words matters. Presenters who shared a stage, a green room or a Saturday-night slot with these men are now being asked what they saw. "Unaware" is a defensible answer for some and a thin one for others, and it will be tested case by case. Ross has his own history here: he was caught up in the 2008 *Sachsgate* row, in which he and Brand left lewd messages on actor Andrew Sachs's answerphone.

The Walliams story is at an earlier stage than Brand's. It rests on journalism and a denial, not a court finding, and police say they have received no related reports so far. Two things will show whether anything beyond statements follows: whether the Met's assessment turns into an investigation, and whether the broadcasters and publishers named in the allegations say what they knew and did.
ross-walliams-brand-fallout.in_one_sentence: Jonathan Ross says he is 'horrified' by the Walliams allegations and Brand's conviction, as police investigate two further alleged rapes by Brand and Walliams denies wrongdoing.

man-utd-monaco-manager-summit.headline: The Monaco summit that will decide the future of Carrick and Man Utd
man-utd-monaco-manager-summit.body_md:
Manchester United's owners and senior executives are due to gather in Monaco on Wednesday to decide whether Michael Carrick keeps the job he was given permanently only in May. If the reporting is right, the real question is who replaces him, and whether a club that has not held a managerial succession together since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013 can get this one right.

The meeting was arranged in advance to use the international break. Co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe will attend, along with chief executive Omar Berrada and technical director Jason Wilcox, according to reports relaying BBC Sport. Berrada and Wilcox are expected to recommend that Carrick be dismissed. Ratcliffe has the final say but is expected to consult the Glazer family. No outcome had been confirmed at the time of writing. If Carrick goes, he would reportedly be told in person in Manchester on Thursday.

## A short tenure, a poor start

Carrick, 45, signed a two-year contract in May 2026 after taking over from Ruben Amorim, who was sacked in January. By the account in the reports, the contract has not bought him patience. United have won one league match this season and sit in the relegation zone, which is described as the club's worst start after ten games in four decades. Those figures come from a single chain of reporting and should be read as such.

A dismissal would cost money. Carrick could receive up to £5m in compensation, a sum that is small by Premier League standards but hard to justify for a man appointed on a permanent basis six months earlier. It is also the second time in a few years that United have turned to a former player to steady things, and the second time the steadying has not lasted.

## The shortlist

Three names appear in the reporting: Mauricio Pochettino, Eddie Howe and Unai Emery.

- **Pochettino** signed a new contract as head coach of the United States men's national team only months ago, but has said openly that he wants to return to Premier League management. Some outlets say the Glazers regard him as their top pick. That is a claim about a preference, not a decision.
- **Howe** is available without a fee, having left Newcastle United in the summer. Earlier reporting described him as fully open to the job if it came up.
- **Emery** won the Europa League with Aston Villa last season and is the third name in the BBC-sourced options. The reporting says little about how seriously he is being considered.

The list is a signal as much as a plan. All three are experienced, Premier League-literate coaches with established methods. That is a different profile from the two most recent appointments, a young and unproven coach followed by a stopgap. It suggests the club wants to buy certainty after a stretch of buying potential.

## The pattern that matters

Since Ferguson retired, United have gone through David Moyes, Louis van Gaal, José Mourinho, Ole Gunnar Solskjær, Ralf Rangnick on an interim basis, Erik ten Hag, Amorim and Carrick. The change of ownership structure under Ratcliffe, with Berrada and Wilcox brought in to run football operations, was meant to end the improvisation. The Monaco meeting is the first real test of that structure under pressure.

Two features of the process are worth noting. The recommendation is coming from the executives, not the owner, which is how a modern football club is supposed to work. But the final call still rests with Ratcliffe, and the Glazers are still consulted, so the old ownership layer has not disappeared. If the Glazers' reported preference for Pochettino carries the day over the executives' own judgment, that would say something about where power actually sits.

Timing adds pressure. United want a new manager in place ideally before the Liverpool match after the international break, which leaves little room for a drawn-out courtship, and particularly little if the preferred candidate is under contract with a national federation.

## What to watch

The first signal is whether Carrick is told on Thursday, as reported. The second is who United approach first, and whether compensation or contract issues, notably Pochettino's deal with US Soccer, slow the process. Howe's availability makes him the simplest option; Pochettino's is the more complicated one. Whoever is in the dugout against Liverpool will show how much of the Monaco meeting was a decision and how much was a hope.
man-utd-monaco-manager-summit.in_one_sentence: United's owners and executives meet in Monaco amid reports that Carrick will be recommended for dismissal, with Pochettino, Howe and Emery named as options; nothing is confirmed.

floor.headline: One oversold bounce carried the day; the rest just sat there
floor.body_md:
Mostly a one-trade day. HOGS.MI did the heavy lifting: a deep-oversold entry recovered about five percent and was banked at midday, before any fade arrived. That is the mean-reversion playbook working as written, though it is only the second bounce on this name in a week, and two is a thin sample.

LEI.DE took its target for a smaller winner. The losers were quiet. NEU and XIFR both reached the scheduled close without a stop firing or a rebound arriving. NEU was stopped out last week, and the selling has eased, but no buyer has appeared to replace it.

Tomorrow's question is whether HOGS.MI bounces a third time, or whether two good entries were all this name had to offer.

floor.headline: Two stops, no survivors: a late TSM entry and a failed AMD.DE gap
floor.body_md:
Two stops, two trades, no survivors. The shadow book's uk-eu sleeve spent the day on the wrong side of two thin bets, and the one that cost more was TSM. The thesis was post-revenue-beat continuation, but the timing was off. The bot bought after the morning move had already run, so it was buying into fade risk rather than momentum. Price slipped about two percent from entry and the stop closed the position.

AMD.DE was a similar story in a different costume. The overnight-gap idea leaned on a single earlier take-profit, which was one instance rather than a pattern. US-session strength never carried into the EU open, and the stop took the position out.

The stops behaved as designed, which is small comfort. Tomorrow's question is whether the gate can tell a headline that is already priced in from one that is still fresh before it commits capital.

floor.headline: Mean-reverters quietly carry the mid-table; ML challenger lags
floor.body_md: Away from the headline movers, two mean-reverters quietly did the heavy lifting. Gap-industry-neutral booked £137.23 from two closes, HOGS.MI and MAKS.MC, averaging +2.41%, the best per-trade figure in the group. Residual-return was close behind, netting £116.22 across three European names (IPOK.DE, LEI.DE, S188.DE) at a +2.00% average. The news-reactive agent's single closed trade, in TSM, added £22.03 (+1.38%). The ML challenger was the laggard: five closes, roughly zero on average, yet down £22.97 in total, a reminder that a flat average can still hide a loss.

floor.headline: COHR +17.8% led US misses; no strategy held a top mover
floor.body_md: COHR led the US misses at +17.8%; no same-day news was found, and the Nov 4 Q1 beat is the only plausible backdrop. No strategy held any of the ten biggest US movers. MPWR (+16%, a sector-beta bounce; some sources date it Nov 9) and TER (+13%, no catalyst found) also ran without a position. FERG (+12.4%) had a real catalyst: a fiscal Q3 beat with FY26 sales guidance raised to about 7%. The missed-movers record is internally inconsistent: its summary says these names cleared the S&P 500 screen, while its per-ticker field lists no universe membership. Until that is resolved, a filter miss cannot be told apart from a coverage gap. AMD's +14.45% looks like a stale-baseline artifact and is left out. NVDA (-4.9%) is beyond a long-only basket.
